lessons.title: Wildlife management in the South African context
lessons.html:
The wildlife sector

The Diploma in Wildlife Management (NQF 6) prepares practitioners for the South African game ranching and conservation sector. This includes national and provincial parks, private reserves, conservancies, game ranches and community conservation areas. Wildlife managers protect biodiversity while enabling sustainable use.

Core knowledge areas

  • Ecology: how plants, animals, soil, water and fire interact. South Africa's biomes include savanna, grassland, Nama-Karoo, Succulent Karoo, fynbos, forest and thicket, each with its own management needs.
  • Wildlife identification and behaviour: mammals, birds, reptiles and key plants, including tracks and signs.
  • Population monitoring: aerial counts, road counts, camera traps, call-up surveys for predators.
  • Habitat management: fire, alien plant control, bush encroachment, erosion, water provision.
  • Animal health and capture: working with vets on immobilisation, translocation and disease testing.

Conservation versus utilisation

Protected areas focus mainly on conserving biodiversity, while game ranches focus on sustainable utilisation such as hunting, live sales and tourism. In practice the two overlap. Biodiversity stewardship programmes allow private and communal land to be declared protected under the National Environmental Management: Protected Areas Act 57 of 2003 while landowners keep ownership. Wildlife economy projects aim to bring benefits to rural communities through employment, game donations and community-owned reserves.

Threats to wildlife

  • Habitat loss and fragmentation from farming, mining and settlements.
  • Poaching, especially of rhino, and bushmeat snaring.
  • Human-wildlife conflict: predators killing livestock, elephants damaging crops.
  • Alien invasive species and diseases.
  • Climate change and drought.

lessons.title: Practical management and compliance
lessons.html:
Day-to-day management

Wildlife managers combine field work with planning and administration. Typical tasks:

  • Fence and road patrols and maintenance.
  • Monitoring waterpoints, veld condition and animal condition.
  • Recording sightings, mortalities and births in a database.
  • Supervising field staff and anti-poaching teams.
  • Arranging game captures and sales with permits.
  • Managing burns under a fire plan with firebreaks and fire protection association rules.

Human-wildlife conflict

Conflict reduces support for conservation. Practical responses include predator-proof kraals and livestock guarding dogs or Anatolian shepherds for neighbouring farmers, early warning systems, maintenance of electrified fences, and compensation or incentive schemes. Damage-causing animals must be handled according to the provincial norms and permits, not by poisoning, which kills non-target species such as vultures.

Statutory compliance

AreaLaw or instrument
Protected and threatened speciesBiodiversity Act 10 of 2004 and TOPS regulations
Protected areasProtected Areas Act 57 of 2003
Environmental authorisationNEMA 107 of 1998
Hunting, keeping and transporting gameProvincial conservation laws
Animal diseasesAnimal Diseases Act 35 of 1984
FirearmsFirearms Control Act 60 of 2000
International tradeCITES through national regulations

Safety in the field

Field work brings risks from dangerous animals, snakes, heat, lightning and vehicles. Always tell someone your route, carry water and a radio or phone, never approach elephants or buffalo on foot without a trained armed guide, and follow the OHS Act 85 of 1993 safety rules of your employer.

Key points

  • Wildlife managers protect biodiversity while enabling sustainable use.
  • Core skills include ecology, identification, monitoring, habitat management and animal health.
  • Biodiversity stewardship lets private land be protected while owners keep ownership.
  • Manage human-wildlife conflict without poisoning.
  • Comply with national and provincial wildlife laws and work safely in the field.
